prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength enable frequency standards of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B041) as my final position, with the same two names, but I do so after testing it against B046 rather than by default. The discovery is concrete and was made by identifiable people: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removed the conflict between holding many atoms for a long time and perturbing the clock transition, and Ye's group took strontium lattice clocks to about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, well beyond caesium and past the best single-ion clocks. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by independent groups and is in routine intercontinental comparison campaigns, so there is no open question about whether the effect is real. It has reach into tests of fundamental constants, dark-matter and variation models and relativistic geodesy. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: all six members who ranked it propose exactly Katori and Ye, and the two names correspond to the concept and the performance record. I sharpened the citation after Lindroth's and Kroll's statements so that it names the lattice scheme and the magic wavelength, which keeps it distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
statement.case_against: The principal objection remains overlap: the 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and laser precision spectroscopy and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped ions for clocks, so a colleague outside atomic physics can read B041 as a refinement of recognised ground. Kroll and Eriksson press this, and I cannot show it is wrong, only that the neutral-atom lattice with its many-atom statistics is a different mechanism. The second has not yet been redefined, so the case rests on demonstrated performance, not adoption. The credit also omits other strontium, ytterbium and aluminium-ion clock groups. Finally, B046 has the broadest opening support, four explicit round-1 supporters against three for B041, and I am aware that as Chair I should not let my own camp's size stand in for the scientific comparison. If the committee judges that opening a new class of correlated materials outweighs another order of magnitude in clock accuracy, B046 is a legitimate choice and I would not resist it.

responses.point: Argues that B046 is the cleanest prediction-then-discovery chain on the shortlist, that opening a new class of correlated materials outweighs a further order of magnitude in clock accuracy, and that B041 may be a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: The prediction-then-discovery chain is real and I give it full weight; that is why B046 is my first alternative. On novelty I disagree with the framing that B041 only refines earlier prizes. The comb supplied a way to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize concerned a single ion; the lattice clock solves a different problem, interrogating many neutral atoms without a trapping shift, and that is what delivered the 1e-18 regime. On breadth of impact I concede your point, since moire materials have spread to many platforms while clocks remain a metrology field. Your own stated uncertainty is that three names cannot represent the experimental side without Cao and the parallel groups, and I find that a heavier attribution cost than anything on B041, where the credit problem is only the other clock groups.

responses.point: Supports B041 with Katori for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for the systematic-uncertainty and coherence record, and has disclosed a research stay in John Hall's laboratory with Jun Ye as a close scientific descendant of that environment.
responses.response: I agree with the division of credit and with your admission that lattice clocks sit close to the 2005 and 2012 lines. Because we are in the same camp, the committee should not read our agreement as independent confirmation, and I would ask that B046 be argued at full strength before the vote. Your Hall-laboratory link is a mentorship tie, not a collaboration, and I think disclosure is sufficient; if colleagues disagree, the decision should be theirs, and the B041 case would survive with one fewer supporter. I do not share your suggestion that the lattice-clock priority details from memory are an obstacle, because the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice-clock demonstrations are well documented in the clock literature.

responses.point: Ranks B046 first as a theoretical prediction followed by a decisive experiment that created a field, and argues the open pairing mechanism does not undermine the discovery of the phases themselves.
responses.response: I accept the central point: the correlated insulating and superconducting phases are reproduced in many laboratories, so the unresolved pairing mechanism does not make the discovery uncertain, and I withdraw part of my round-1 emphasis on that. What remains for me is attribution and timing. Yuan Cao as first author, and the Dean, Yacoby and Young groups, are outside the trio, and a citation that says the Jarillo-Herrero group is a workable but imperfect fix. Eight years is short. I would not call it disqualifying, but I weigh it against a clock programme reproduced for over a decade. We differ in weighting, and I do not claim your weighting is wrong.

responses.point: Keeps dynamical mean-field theory (B001) as his configuration on grounds of conceptual originality and thirty years of confirmation, while acknowledging that Metzner is outside the credited trio and that it may be seen as a method.
responses.response: The durability of DMFT is the strongest maturity case on the shortlist and I do not dispute the physics. My difficulty is the one you name yourself: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit, so a trio that omits Metzner is hard to defend, and a three-name limit offers no way to add him without dropping Georges, Kotliar or Vollhardt. Whether the prize rewards a method or a discovery of nature I leave to the committee, but the attribution gap decides it for me. I also note that you list B041 as your first alternative, which shows that its credit structure is not in dispute even among members who rank it lower.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as a sufficiently distinct step beyond the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is the point I cannot settle by argument alone.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second or recognise the demonstrated 1e-18 performance now.
Whether other strontium, ytterbium and aluminium-ion clock groups make the two-name credit indefensible on a careful reading of the history.
Whether about eight years since the 2018 experiment is enough maturity for B046, which would decide whether I could move to it.
Priority details for the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice-clock demonstrations rest on my reading of the supplied material and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B041 from my documented record. For disclosure, B033 (IceCube) lies in my own field of astroparticle physics and I know the Fermi-LAT, PAMELA and multi-messenger community, so I remain willing to recuse from any decision on B033, which is now only an alternative. I also note Kroll's disclosed Hall-laboratory link to B041 and consider disclosure sufficient, but I would accept the committee's judgement on recusal. I record no tie to any B046 name.
